title: Person or Setting? Workplace Explanation Laboratory
summary: Evidence about one fictional team arrives in two rounds, and you commit to an explanation after each. Then spend a budget across three levels and see what your combination leaves in force.
learningObjectives: Construct individual, relational and organisational explanations of the same workplace problem.
Explain why a real, replicable difference between people does not locate its own cause.
State what each intervention targets and precisely what it leaves in place.
Judge the limits of a matched-team comparison that was matched at recruitment and is not matched now.
Resist both the claim that psychological intervention is a distraction and the claim that structural explanation always wins.
interactionTypes: staged evidence release with a recorded answer trail
costed intervention selection against a budget
bar chart with full text equivalent
privacy: Every selection is held in the browser tab only and discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted, and no score or judgement about the person using it is produced.
accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed. All controls are native radios, checkboxes and buttons in labelled fieldsets, and committing with nothing selected produces an explanatory message that treats 'several at once' as a real answer. Evidence released in the second round carries a heavier left rule, but each item states its own number and the round heading names what has just arrived, so nothing is carried by the rule alone. Interventions the remaining budget cannot cover are disabled, dimmed, and say so in their own cost line rather than relying on opacity. The outcome chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence giving the before and after scores, the comparison team and the cost; every value is also printed beside its own bar. Both experiments announce every change through the shell's polite live region, and either reset button restores the entire page including the prediction gate and the other experiment. Headings run h1 to h5 without skipping, focus moves to the first experiment's heading when the gate opens, the stage track carries aria-current with a done state in text, targets are at least 2.75rem, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths. Experiment 1 is exactly two rounds, so the commit-and-reveal cycle is short and the round title states what has just been added. The tried-combinations table has four columns (combination, cost, levels, exhaustion) that fit without horizontal scrolling at narrow widths.
readmeTopic: A correlation of 0.61 inside one team, a rota that is the same for all fourteen, and a budget that covers half of what is needed
simulationNotes: Kelbridge Service Centre, its two teams, its review, its exhaustion scale and all its figures were written for this page; no real organisation, team, incident, instrument or person is described, and no number is a norm, a prevalence or a published effect. Nothing is random. Experiment 1 releases evidence in exactly two rounds: round 1 is four individual-level items; round 2 releases the remaining seven items at once - the team's norms and supervision together with the rota, the queue, the target and a matched comparison team at 38 against Team B's 74 - so the reversal from a person-level to a setting-level reading lands once, on the evidence that settles it, rather than being split across a separate relational round and a separate structural round. The explanation feedback differs by round and by answer, and round 1 treats the individual-level answer as the best-supported reading of the evidence available, because it is. The finer question of whether the relational mechanisms cause the exhaustion or carry it is argued in the debrief rather than asked as a third judgement. Experiment 2 starts at a team mean of 74 on a 0-100 scale and subtracts each selected intervention's effect: resilience workshops 6 (halved to 3 when nothing structural is also chosen, because the conditions that produced the exhaustion go on producing it), coaching for two 1, weekly protected debrief 9, supervisor feedback practice 8, rota and recovery redesign 18, target and discretion change 16. There are no pair bonuses and no projected-leavers figure: the panel reports one modelled after-score and the list of evidence the chosen combination leaves in force, because the question is what an account of the problem makes somebody buy rather than which package scores best. Costs are 2, 2, 3, 3, 5 and 5 against a budget of 10, so all six together (20 units) are unreachable by design. The two ten-unit extremes reach 53 (the individual and relational interventions together) and 40 (the two structural interventions alone). That the structural combination outperforms is true by construction and is stated as such on the page; the evidence about what works in real workplaces is in the literature, not here.
